result.title: Ode to Joy
result.teacher_note: Keep your hand relaxed and let each group of four notes flow evenly; the common stumble is the longer note near the end of the first line, so count it carefully instead of rushing. Once the right hand feels easy, try a simple left-hand pulse on C and G with single whole notes or blocked fifths.
result.listen_for: It is recognisable from the smooth stepwise rise and fall of the opening phrase starting E E F G.

result.title: Greensleeves
result.teacher_note: Let the long notes sing, especially the opening G and the high D, because that rise-and-fall shape gives the tune its wistful feeling. The usual stumble is around the dotted rhythms like B4:1.5 C5:0.5, so count them carefully as "long-short" instead of rushing. Once the right hand feels easy, try a very simple left hand with single bass notes on G and D underneath the stronger beats.
result.listen_for: The melody is recognisable from its opening climb E-G-A-B and the graceful drop back down afterward.

result.title: Scarborough Fair
result.teacher_note: Let the long notes sing and keep a gentle 3-beat waltz pulse underneath: count '1-2-3, 1-2-3' all the way through. The usual stumble is the move up to D5 and E5, so practise that middle phrase slowly in small chunks; once the right hand feels easy, the left hand can simply play single bass notes on beat 1 of each bar, such as E then B then A.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable sound comes from the haunting rise from E up to B and then the higher peak at E5 in a calm waltz flow.

result.title: Für Elise, opening
result.teacher_note: Keep the first five notes light and even, then let the little drop to B-D-C-A sing out as one shape rather than four separate pokes. The usual trip-up is the jump down to C4-E4-A4, so practise that move slowly a few times by itself; once the right hand feels easy, the left hand can simply add single A and E bass notes underneath.
result.listen_for: The recognisable sound comes from the repeated E–D# turn at the start, followed by the falling B–D–C–A answer.

result.title: Amazing Grace
result.teacher_note: Keep the beat steady and let the longer notes sing; this tune sounds best when you avoid rushing the ends of phrases. The usual tricky spot is the move up to D5 and back down, so practise that small group slowly first. Once the right hand feels easy, the left hand can simply play single G notes or broken G and D chords underneath.
result.listen_for: The melody is recognisable from its calm opening rise and the long held notes at the ends of each phrase.

artifact.title: Amazing Grace
artifact.attribution: Traditional hymn tune, text by John Newton (1779), melody 'New Britain' traditional

result.title: The Entertainer (main strain opening)
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist loose and let the short ragtime notes bounce lightly rather than poking at them. The usual trip-up is the little descending pattern crossing from the upper notes down toward middle C, so practise that in small groups of four notes. Once the right hand feels easy, try a simple left-hand steady oom-pah on low D then A to feel the ragtime character.
result.listen_for: The jaunty syncopated drop from the high opening notes into the lower reply is what makes this strain instantly recognisable.

result.title: Danny Boy
result.teacher_note: Let the long notes sing, especially the high peaks, and keep your fingers close to the keys so the leaps feel calmer. Most beginners trip over the jump up to the higher G and the following step down, so practise just that little group a few times on its own. Once the right hand feels easy, add a very simple left hand by holding single bass notes or open fifths on G and D underneath the longer melody notes.
result.listen_for: The tune is recognisable because it rises gently at first, then opens into those broad, emotional long notes at the top of the phrase.

result.title: Twinkle Twinkle Little Star
result.teacher_note: Keep your hand relaxed and let each pair of repeated notes sound even. The usual tricky spot is the change from A down to G, and later from E down to D, so practise those little step-downs slowly first. Once the right hand feels easy, try the left hand playing single bass notes C for the first line, F for the second, and G then C for the ending.
result.listen_for: The melody is recognisable because it begins with the simple leap up from C to G and the matching repeated-note pattern in each phrase.

result.title: Auld Lang Syne
result.teacher_note: Keep a gentle, singing pulse and let the longer notes breathe, especially at the ends of phrases. The usual trip-up is the small climb into D5 and E5, so practise that bar slowly and keep your fingers close to the keys. Once the right hand feels easy, add simple left-hand single bass notes on strong beats: G for the opening, then D, then back to G.
result.listen_for: The tune is recognisable from its opening rise from D up to G and the long, held E near the middle of each phrase.

result.title: House of the Rising Sun
result.teacher_note: Keep the line smooth and a little mournful rather than choppy; the longer notes are where the tune breathes. Beginners often rush from B4 up to C5 and back, so pause enough to feel that small rise and fall. Once your right hand is comfortable, let the left hand quietly pulse single bass notes or broken A-minor and E-major chords underneath.
result.listen_for: The melody is recognisable from its plaintive climb up to C5 and the answering fall back down.

result.title: Canon in D (opening simple line)
result.teacher_note: Keep the notes very even and legato, almost like you are singing one long sentence. Beginners often rush the climb up to A4, so count steadily and let the longer notes settle; once your right hand is comfortable, try a very simple left hand by holding single bass notes D-A-B-F# underneath in slow whole notes.
result.listen_for: The recognisable sound comes from the smooth descending-and-rising stepwise shape over the famous Canon harmony.

result.title: Silent Night
result.teacher_note: Keep the melody very smooth and gentle, almost like singing a lullaby. The trickiest spot is where it climbs up to E5 and then walks back down, so practise that small section by itself before joining it up. Once your right hand feels easy, try a simple left hand with single bass notes on beat 1 of each bar.
result.listen_for: The recognisable shape comes from the calm repeated opening note and the warm rise to the higher phrase in the middle.

result.title: Clair de Lune (opening phrase, simplified melody)
result.teacher_note: Keep your hand relaxed and let the line feel like one long breath rather than separate taps. The usual snag is the gentle rise to Ab and the return back down without tensing up, so practise that small arch a few times on its own. Once the right hand feels easy, try adding very soft left-hand single bass notes or broken chords on the long beats to support the moonlit feel.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable sound comes from the smooth, floating stepwise rise to the high note and the equally gentle fall back down.

result.title: Moonlight Sonata — First Movement Theme
result.teacher_note: Keep your hand relaxed and let the notes flow very evenly, almost like a quiet bell pattern rather than separate pokes. The usual sticking point is the repeated broken-chord shape: practise each 5-note group slowly until you can land the top note without tension. Once the right hand feels easy, let the left hand simply play single low bass notes on the first beat of each group.
result.listen_for: What makes it recognisable is the steady triplet-like broken-chord motion and the dark, hushed rise to the top note of each pattern.

result.title: Gymnopédie No. 1 (opening melody)
result.teacher_note: Keep the hand loose and let each two-beat note sing; this melody works best when it feels calm rather than strict. The usual stumble is around the turn back down from B4 to A4 to G4, so practise that little three-note shape on its own. Once the right hand is comfortable, add a very simple left-hand pulse on low Gs or open fifths to suggest Satie’s gentle accompaniment.
result.listen_for: The recognisable sound is the slow, floating stepwise rise D–E–F#–G repeated like a quiet question.

result.title: Prelude in C (opening pattern)
result.teacher_note: Keep your hand soft and let each group of eight notes flow like one smooth gesture rather than eight separate pokes. The usual trip-up is reaching too tensely for the top note, so stay close to the keys and rotate the wrist a little as the pattern rises and falls. Once the right hand feels easy, let the left hand quietly play the bass roots underneath as single whole notes: C, D, G, A, C, G, C.
result.listen_for: What makes it recognisable is the continuous broken-chord ripple that gently changes harmony every bar.

result.title: Jingle Bells
result.teacher_note: Keep the repeated E notes light and even, then let the longer notes ring so the tune sounds bouncy instead of choppy. Most beginners stumble where the melody drops to C and climbs back through D to E, so practise that little turn slowly a few times. Once the right hand feels easy, try tapping a steady left-hand beat on low C or G with each bar.
result.listen_for: The tune is recognisable from the opening run of repeated E notes followed by the jump up to G and the walk C–D–E.

result.title: When the Saints Go Marching In
result.teacher_note: Keep the rhythm bouncy and march-like rather than heavy. The usual sticky spot is repeating the opening pattern evenly, so count out loud and let the longer notes ring. Once the right hand feels easy, try simple left-hand bass notes on C for the first phrase and G before you return to C.
result.listen_for: The recognisable sound comes from the repeated rising opening phrase that climbs up to G like a little parade call.

result.title: Swan Lake – Main Theme
result.teacher_note: Keep the hand relaxed and let the long notes sing; this melody sounds best when each 2-beat note has a gentle, sustained tone. The usual trip-up is the F# and C#, so notice they both belong to D major. Once the right hand feels easy, try the left hand with single bass notes on the first beat of each bar: D, A, B, G.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable shape comes from the rising minor-feeling leap into a long note, followed by the smooth stepwise fall.

result.title: In the Hall of the Mountain King
result.teacher_note: Keep the repeated four-note idea very even at first, then let the built-in creep of excitement come from clean repetition rather than rushing. Most beginners stumble where the pattern starts climbing higher, so practise the A-B-C-A shape and then the C-D-E shape separately. Once the right hand feels easy, try a simple left hand with single low A notes on the strong beats.
result.listen_for: The melody is recognisable because of its sneaky repeated rising pattern that keeps returning before climbing a little higher each time.

result.title: The Blue Danube (opening phrase)
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist loose for the little three-note pickups, and aim for a gentle waltz lilt rather than playing everything heavily. The usual trip-up is the quick half-beat notes before each longer note, so count '1-and-2' carefully. Once the right hand feels easy, add a simple left-hand waltz pattern: low bass note on beat 1, then two light chord taps on beats 2 and 3.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable sound comes from the lilting 3/4 waltz pulse and the rising arpeggio shapes that sweep upward through the opening.

result.title: Air on the G String (opening phrase)
result.teacher_note: Keep the hand relaxed and aim for a smooth, singing line with no gaps between notes. The usual tricky spot is the move around B4 to C5 and back down, so practise that little turn slowly first. Once the right hand feels easy, add a very simple left hand by holding single D or G bass notes for two beats at a time.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable character comes from the calm stepwise rise and fall and the long, lyrical note values.

result.title: Habanera (opening phrase)
result.teacher_note: Keep the fingers close to the keys and aim for a smooth, slightly teasing character rather than playing it heavily. The common trip-up is repeating the A cleanly before stepping down; once the right hand feels easy, try a very simple left hand with single bass notes on the first beat of each bar.
result.listen_for: Its recognisable sound comes from the sultry rise to A and the repeated-note pattern that then curls downward step by step.

result.title: Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2 — opening theme
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist loose and let this sing like a voice rather than poking each note. The usual trip-up is overholding while the melody turns back on itself, so practise in tiny 3- to 4-note groups and aim for a smooth connection. Once the right hand feels easy, the left hand can simply place soft broken E-flat major chords underneath on each beat.
result.listen_for: The recognisable sound is the gentle, ornamented rise and fall around G–A–G, with the melody leaning expressively into longer held notes.

result.title: Minuet in G
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist loose and aim for a light, dance-like touch rather than playing it heavily. The usual trip-up is the climb up to F# and G near the middle, so practise that little rise separately until it feels easy. Once the right hand is comfortable, the left hand can add simple single bass notes on the first beat of each bar: G, D, G, D.
result.listen_for: The tune is recognisable from its tidy stepwise opening and the little lift up to the higher G in the middle.

result.title: William Tell Overture – Finale (opening theme)
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist light and let the repeated bounce between E and G feel springy rather than hammered. The usual sticking point is the quick move up to B4 and then C5, so practise just those four-note groups slowly before linking them. Once the right hand feels easy, the left hand can simply play single bass notes on the first beat of each bar—try C, G, C, G—to give it that galloping energy.
result.listen_for: What makes it recognisable is the bright repeated-note fanfare shape that climbs from E–G patterns into the higher B and C before landing firmly back down.

result.title: Für Elise – middle section theme
result.teacher_note: Keep the wrist loose and let the short pickup notes lead into the longer beats instead of accenting every note the same. The usual trip-up is the G-sharp appearing in the second half, so notice that color change early; once the right hand feels easy, try holding simple left-hand A bass notes under each bar.
result.listen_for: What makes this section recognizable is the rising A-minor shape that keeps returning, then the brief brighter twist with G-sharp before it settles back.

result.title: La Cucaracha
result.teacher_note: Keep the repeated C notes light and steady, then let the jump up to F and A feel like the tune opening out. Most beginners rush the repeated notes or hesitate at the A, so practise just those two-bar shapes first; once the right hand feels easy, try a left-hand pulse on low C for each beat.
result.listen_for: The tune is recognisable from its three repeated opening notes followed by the cheerful leap upward.
